notes: Style Guide text: one entry per fabric in taxonomy.json (by id) and the colour basics. General guidance, not product claims. Seasons use taxonomy.json season ids. Edit freely; ids are stable keys.

fabrics.feel: Soft and breathable, and it soaks up sweat. Crisp when woven, stretchy when knitted.
fabrics.care: Machine wash cool or warm. Hot water and a hot dryer can shrink it. Iron while slightly damp for a crisp finish.
fabrics.label: 100% cotton breathes best. Combed or long-staple cotton feels smoother and pills less. For T-shirts, a higher GSM (grams per square metre) means a thicker, longer-lasting fabric.
fabrics.watch: It dries slowly, so heavy cotton can stay damp through a humid monsoon day.

fabrics.feel: Cool, dry, and very breathable, with a slightly textured hand. It softens with every wash.
fabrics.care: Wash gently and hang to dry. Iron while damp if you want it crisp; soft creases are part of the look.
fabrics.label: 100% linen is the coolest. A linen and cotton blend creases less and costs less.
fabrics.watch: It creases as soon as you sit down. Choose a blend for long days at a desk.

fabrics.feel: Sturdy cotton twill. Stiff at first, then it softens and shapes to you.
fabrics.care: Wash inside out in cold water, and not too often, to keep the colour. Dark indigo can stain light fabrics at first.
fabrics.label: One or two per cent elastane (stretch) adds comfort. Raw or selvedge denim is unwashed and fades with wear.
fabrics.watch: Heavy and slow to dry, so it's hard work in the monsoon and hot in summer.

fabrics.feel: Warm without being stuffy, springy, and slow to crease or hold odours.
fabrics.care: Hand wash in cold water or dry clean, and dry flat. Never tumble dry: heat and agitation shrink it.
fabrics.label: Merino is fine and rarely itchy. In a blend, the share of wool decides how warm it is.
fabrics.watch: Moths like it. Store it clean and folded.

fabrics.feel: Made of looped yarn rather than woven threads, so it stretches and drapes: T-shirts, polos, sweaters.
fabrics.care: Dry sweaters flat so they keep their shape, and fold heavy knits instead of hanging them.
fabrics.label: Knit is how it's made, not what it's made of: check the fibre (cotton, wool, acrylic). A tight, even knit pills less.
fabrics.watch: Loose knits snag on watches and bag straps.

fabrics.feel: Smooth and strong. It holds its shape, barely creases, and dries fast.
fabrics.care: Machine wash and dry on low heat. A hot iron can melt or shine it.
fabrics.label: In a blend (poly-cotton) it adds crease resistance. For hot days, look for more cotton or linen in the mix.
fabrics.watch: It doesn't breathe like natural fibres, so it traps heat and can hold on to odours.

fabrics.feel: Soft and cool, with a fluid drape. Made from wood pulp.
fabrics.care: Delicate when wet: hand wash or use a gentle cycle in cold water, and don't wring it. It can shrink.
fabrics.label: Viscose, rayon, modal, and lyocell are related. Modal and lyocell are usually stronger and keep their shape better.
fabrics.watch: Cheap viscose loses its shape after a few washes.

fabrics.feel: Light and smooth with a soft sheen. Cool in the heat and warm in the cold.
fabrics.care: Dry clean, or hand wash in cold water with a mild detergent. Keep it out of direct sun, and put perfume on before you dress.
fabrics.label: Pure silk is the real thing. Art silk is artificial silk, usually viscose or polyester.
fabrics.watch: Water and sweat can leave marks.

fabrics.feel: Glossy on the face and dull on the back. Satin is a weave, so it can be silk, polyester, or a blend.
fabrics.care: Follow the fibre: usually a gentle wash or dry cleaning. Iron on the dull side, on low.
fabrics.label: Silk satin breathes. Polyester satin is cheaper and warmer.
fabrics.watch: It snags easily and shows every crease.

fabrics.feel: Tough and supple. Good leather shapes to you and ages well.
fabrics.care: Wipe clean and condition now and then. Let wet shoes dry away from direct heat, and use shoe trees.
fabrics.label: Full-grain leather is the most durable. "Genuine leather" is a lower grade. PU or faux leather is a plastic coating on fabric.
fabrics.watch: Soaking in heavy rain can stain it and stiffen it.

fabrics.feel: The soft, brushed underside of leather. Velvety and less formal than smooth leather.
fabrics.care: Brush it with a suede brush and use a protector spray before the first wear.
fabrics.label: Nubuck looks similar but is buffed from the outer side, so it wears a little better.
fabrics.watch: Water leaves marks. Keep it for dry days.

fabrics.feel: Heavy, plain-woven cotton or a blend. Sturdy and casual: sneakers, bags, jackets.
fabrics.care: Spot clean or wash gently, and air dry. Heat can shrink it and loosen glued soles.
fabrics.label: Thicker canvas lasts longer.
fabrics.watch: It soaks up rain and dries slowly.

fabrics.feel: Performance fabrics, often nylon or polyester with a finish: water-resistant, quick-drying, stretchy.
fabrics.care: Wash cool and skip fabric softener: it clogs the finish that wicks sweat and sheds water.
fabrics.label: Water-resistant sheds a shower. Waterproof, with taped seams, keeps out real rain.
fabrics.watch: It can feel clammy in the heat when it doesn't breathe.

fabrics.feel: Two or more fibres together, mixing their traits: a poly-cotton shirt creases less than cotton and breathes better than polyester.
fabrics.care: Follow the care label; it's set by the most delicate fibre.
fabrics.label: Fibres are listed largest share first, with percentages. The first one tells you most about how it will feel.
fabrics.watch: A little of a fibre adds little. Five per cent cashmere won't make a jumper warm.

colour.title: Neutrals do most of the work
colour.text: Neutrals go with nearly anything, so most outfits are built on them and one piece carries the colour. These are the colours WearWise treats as neutral.

colour.title: How many colours
colour.text: Neutrals don't count. One or two colours on a neutral base look deliberate; three or more start to compete, and WearWise scores an outfit lower when they do. Shades of one colour count as one.

colour.title: Light against dark
colour.text: Two neutrals look sharpest with clear contrast in lightness, like navy and white. Two shades that are close but not the same, like two slightly different blues, can look like a near miss rather than a choice.

colour.title: Colours together
colour.text: Neighbouring colours (blue and teal) blend easily. Opposite colours (blue and orange) balance well when one or both are soft; two strong opposites make a bold look.

colour.title: Match your leathers
colour.text: A leather belt and leather shoes in the same colour, brown with brown or black with black, look sharper. WearWise notes it when they're clearly different.

colour.title: One metal
colour.text: A watch, a buckle, and jewellery in one metal, silver or gold, read as a set. Mixing is a choice to make on purpose.
